candidate_sources.title: Colletotrichum musae (tip rot of banana)
candidate_sources.snippet: On banana fruits the fungus causes sunken lesions, which turn into sunken, dark patches with orange acervuli as the fruit ripens. Anthracnose is a latent infection where fungal spores infect immature banana in the field but symptoms do not appear until ripening. Tip rot symptoms develop from decaying floral parts. Management encompasses cultural, chemical, natural products, biological, and genetic resistance.

candidate_sources.title: Characterisation of Colletotrichum Species Associated with Anthracnose of Banana
candidate_sources.snippet: Colletotrichum musae causes a latent (quiescent) infection in immature fruits, with symptoms gradually developing as the fruits ripen, producing black or brown sunken spots bearing masses of salmon-colored acervuli with conidia on the fruit peel after ripening.

candidate_sources.title: Thiophanate-Methyl Resistance and Fitness Components of Colletotrichum musae Isolates from Banana in Brazil | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose, caused by Colletotrichum musae, is the most important postharvest disease of banana. Study of fungicide (thiophanate-methyl) resistance and fitness of C. musae isolates relevant to postharvest management of banana anthracnose.

candidate_sources.title: Colletotrichum musae - Wikipedia
candidate_sources.snippet: Colletotrichum musae is a plant pathogen primarily affecting bananas and plantains, best known as a cause of anthracnose (black and brown spots) on bananas. Symptoms appear as dark brown/black sunken lesions with orange fungal growth (acervuli) in the centre, and premature ripening of fruit. Favorable conditions include high humidity and 25–30 °C.

candidate_sources.title: Banana Bunchy Top: Detailed Signs and Symptoms (CTAHR, University of Hawaii)
candidate_sources.snippet: The most characteristic symptoms are short, dark-green dots and dashes ("Morse-code" pattern) along the minor leaf veins, hooks curving downwards near the midrib. Plants are stunted with short, bunched, upright chlorotic leaves and rarely produce fruit.

candidate_sources.title: Fact sheet - Banana bunchy top (121) - Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds (Lucid)
candidate_sources.snippet: Banana bunchy top disease is caused by a single-strand DNA virus, the banana bunchy top virus, spread by the aphid Pentalonia nigronervosa. Plants show stunted, short, bunched leaves with the characteristic dot-dash (Morse-code) pattern; leaf edges roll upwards with yellow margins. Management includes virus-free planting material, roguing, and vector control.

candidate_sources.title: Banana bunchy top virus (bunchy top of banana) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Banana bunchy top virus (BBTV; genus Babuvirus, family Nanoviridae) is a serious pathogen of banana (AAA genome) and plantain (AAB genome). Transmitted in a persistent, circulative manner by the banana aphid Pentalonia nigronervosa. Symptoms include dark green streaks, chlorotic upright leaves clustered into a bunchy top, stunting, and cessation of fruiting.

candidate_sources.title: Cigar End Rot | Pests & Diseases | Plantix
candidate_sources.snippet: Cigar end rot is a disease of banana caused mainly by the fungus Trachysphaera fructigena and sometimes another fungus (Verticillium theobromae). Symptoms develop as a dry, gray to black rot at the tip of the fruits; the tip of infected fingers later gets covered with a powdery mass of spores resembling the grey ash end of a cigar. Spores are spread by air currents and infection is common in the early days of fruit emergence; optimum temperature and high relative humidity are necessary for infection.

candidate_sources.title: Cigar end rot | Infonet Biovision Home
candidate_sources.snippet: Cigar end rot of banana causes a dry rot of the flower end that produces an ash grey wrinkled lesion on the banana fingers, similar to the burnt end of a cigar. The pathogen enters the banana finger through the flower, causing a dry rot of immature fingers. In storage or during transport the disease may progress to involve the whole fruit. Management includes removing bracts/pistils, opening up bunches, and bunch covers.

candidate_sources.title: Cigar End Rot Of Banana | Greenlife
candidate_sources.snippet: Cigar end rot is a disease of banana caused by the fungi Verticillium theobromae and Trachysphaera fructigena. Symptoms include blackening and folding of banana finger tips, giving them a corrugated and ash-covered appearance resembling a cigar. The disease favors high rainfall, humidity, and temperatures between 18-22 C; the fungus attacks at the flowering stage. Management: removing bracts/pistils, opening bunches, and fungicide sprays.

candidate_sources.title: Trachysphaera fructigena - Wikipedia
candidate_sources.snippet: Trachysphaera fructigena is a fungal plant pathogen that causes cigar-end rot of banana, in which the dried, blackened flower end of the fruit resembles the ash of a cigar. It also causes mealy pod disease of cocoa. The disease may act together with Verticillium theobromae (Musicillium theobromae).

candidate_sources.title: Cordana leaf spot | Improving the understanding of banana
candidate_sources.snippet: Two Neocordana species are responsible for Cordana leaf spot symptoms: Neocordana musae, formerly Cordana musae and originally described as Scoletrichum musae; and Neocordana johnstonii. Leaf spots (up to 10 cm), oval to diamond-shaped and pale brown with a yellow border, appear on the upper leaf side. Common worldwide but generally little impact on production.

candidate_sources.title: Insight into Antifungal Metabolites from Bacillus stercoris 92p Against Banana Cordana Leaf Spot Caused by Neocordana musae
candidate_sources.snippet: Cordana leaf spot caused by Neocordana musae; inoculum spread through splashing water and wind, devastating in closely planted fields; growth and spread accelerated by frequent rain and hot, humid conditions; biocontrol strategies discussed.

candidate_sources.title: Cordana leaf spot | Disease Treatment | Bayer Crop Science
candidate_sources.snippet: Cordana leaf spot of banana: oval to diamond-shaped pale brown spots with yellow border; management includes removing infected leaves, monitoring and applying registered fungicide, proper spacing to avoid mutual shading, and avoiding sprinkler irrigation.

candidate_sources.title: Neocordana musae - Wikipedia
candidate_sources.snippet: Neocordana musae (formerly Cordana musae) is a fungal plant pathogen causing Cordana leaf spot of banana.

candidate_sources.title: Postharvest Rots of Banana
candidate_sources.snippet: Most postharvest diseases of bananas are fungal rots in the stalks and crowns, caused by Colletotrichum musae and several Fusarium species. Crown rot brings about softening and darkening of the crown region and detachment of the fruit; management involves packing station sanitation and reduction of wounding during harvest and packaging.

candidate_sources.title: Banana (Cavendish) | Postharvest Research and Extension Center, UC Davis
candidate_sources.snippet: Postharvest pathology of banana includes crown rot and anthracnose. Crown rot is caused by a fungal complex including Colletotrichum musae, Lasiodiplodia theobromae, Thielaviopsis paradoxa, and Fusarium verticillioides; control involves sanitation, fungicide treatment of the cut crown, and careful handling.

candidate_sources.title: Crown Rot of Bananas: Preharvest Factors Involved in Postharvest Disease Development and Integrated Control Methods (Plant Disease, APS)
candidate_sources.snippet: Crown rot is a complex postharvest disease affecting export bananas in all banana-producing countries. Symptoms occur during shipment, ripening, and storage; the crown tissue becomes black and soft and is often covered with white mycelia. Colletotrichum musae is the most commonly isolated and most pathogenic fungus, with Musicillium theobromae, Ceratocystis paradoxa, Lasiodiplodia theobromae, and Fusarium species also contributing.

candidate_sources.title: Black Sigatoka — APSnet Plant Disease Lessons
candidate_sources.snippet: The first symptoms of black Sigatoka disease are tiny, chlorotic spots that appear on the bottom (abaxial) surface of the 3rd or 4th open leaf. The spots grow into thin brown streaks limited by leaf veins, darken with a purple tinge, then enlarge into fusiform/elliptical black streaks. Caused by the ascomycete fungus Pseudocercospora fijiensis (Mycosphaerella fijiensis); spread by wind, rain and irrigation splash. The most damaging disease of banana and plantain, reducing bunch weight up to 50%.

candidate_sources.title: Mycosphaerella fijiensis (black Sigatoka) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Black sigatoka is a leaf-spot disease of banana plants caused by the ascomycete fungus Mycosphaerella fijiensis (Morelet), also known as black leaf streak. Musa spp. and Heliconia psittacorum are the main hosts. One of the most important diseases of banana worldwide, causing up to 50% yield loss; control is primarily through extensive fungicide application (25–30% of production cost). Datasheet covers Identity, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Impacts, and Prevention/Control.

candidate_sources.title: Black Leaf Streak or Sigatoka Disease — Key Pests and Pathogens of Banana (CTAHR Banana IPM Guidebook)
candidate_sources.snippet: Chapter II of the University of Hawaii CTAHR Banana IPM Guidebook covering Black Leaf Streak (Sigatoka) disease — symptoms, pathogen biology, disease cycle, and integrated management recommendations for banana growers.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense (Panama disease of banana) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: The CABI Compendium datasheet on Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense covers Identity, Overview, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Natural Enemies, Impacts, Prevention/Control, and Further Information.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Wilt of Banana | Phytopathology - APS Journals
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense causes a typical wilt syndrome on infected banana plants accompanied by necrosis and rotting of roots, rhizome, and pseudostem vessels. Management is largely restricted to excluding F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense from noninfested areas and using resistant cultivars.

candidate_sources.title: Agnote No: I51 - Fusarium Wilt of Bananas (Panama Disease)
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium wilt of bananas (Panama disease) extension Agnote covering causes, symptoms (leaf yellowing, vascular discoloration), pathogen Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense, races, and management/phytosanitary control measures.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense (E. F. Sm.) W. C. — Tropical Race 4 datasheet
candidate_sources.snippet: Purdue CAPS datasheet on Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense Tropical Race 4 (Foc TR4), the strain threatening Cavendish banana, with identification, hosts, distribution and management.
